utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, November 20th, 2008. Good morning to the witness. Good morning to the OTP representatives. Good morning to Mr. Seselj, and good morning to everyone assisting us in this case. Before I ask the witness to take the solemn declaration, I'm going to refer to two decisions that will be filed in a few minutes. I'm going to read out the operative part of these decisions, because the decisions, as such, are quite long. So I'm not going to read them out in their entirety. I'm just going to read out the operative part of these decisions. The first ruling relates to the motion of the OTP to apply 92 ter to VS-1035. The Trial Chamber dismisses the Prosecutor's motion and decides, first of all, to hear Witness VS-1035 viva voce, and to grant one hour and a half to the Prosecution and an hour and a half to the accused for the purpose of the cross-examination. That's what I had to say for Witness VS-1035. Now, decision related to the Prosecution's motion to hear Witness Sulejman Tihic pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Trial Chamber has ruled as follows: The Trial Chamber dismisses the motion and decides, first of all, to hear Witness Sulejman Tihic viva voce, and to give an hour to the Prosecution and one hour to the accused. That's all. These decisions will be translated in due course, but I wanted to inform you all about these decisions immediately. Witness, would you please stand. Please state your last name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anna-Maria Radic. I was born on the 2nd of September, 1969, in Germany, Florsheim.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm head of the Administration for Areas of Special State Concern in the Ministry of Regional Development of Forestry and Water Management of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, have you ever testified before a court of law with respect to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is it going to be the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Let me give you some information about the way we are going to proceed, because we don't want you to be surprised by what's going to happen at any point in time. First of all, you will have to answer questions put to you by the representative of the OTP. You've probably met her before coming to testify here. She will put a number of questions to you, based on your report and based most probably on a number of documents that will be shown to you. During that phase of the proceedings, it may very well happen that the three Judges sitting before you ask you follow-up questions in order to further explore some of the topics you examine in your report. As a rule, this first stage of the testimony runs extremely smoothly for the witness. But when it comes to the second stage of the testimony, to the cross-examination, it may be rather trying for the witness, because the Defence cross-examining the Prosecution witness inevitably asks questions related to the credibility of the witness and to the substance of the statement of the witness or of the report of the witness, when the witness is an expert witness. As a result, this part of the testimony may be trying, but that's the way things have been provided for by the Rules. Since you are dealing here in your testimony with technical matters, I'm going to ask you, Witness, to be as specific as possible in your answers. If a question is not clear enough to you, please ask the one asking the question to rephrase it. We have breaks every 90 minutes. We'll have our first break of 20 minutes at 10.00 a.m., and then we'll have a second break later. We have an hour and 20 minutes before the first break, and Ms. Biersay will most probably be able to complete her examination-in-chief before the break. I wanted to tell you all this for your testimony to run as smoothly as possible. Ms. Biersay, good morning again, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you please give the Court the full name of the organisation for which you work currently?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Currently, I work for the Ministry of Regional Development. Within that Ministry, there is the Department for Areas of Special State Concern. It's recently changed as far as its name is concerned. It was called the Administration for the Return of Displaced Persons, Returnees and Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that entity the successor entity to the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in abbreviated form, is it often referred to as the ODPR?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if I use that acronym, ODPR, can we agree that it would include your current place of employment as well as all the predecessor entities?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You prepared a report for this case, the Seselj case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was that a report that was limited to the Seselj case or was it also prepared with consideration for another case?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: It was prepared with another case in mind, Simatovic. It's another case that has yet to start. So, in fact, I drafted one single report, since according to the requests of the Prosecution in another case, the subject I had to deal with overlapped. So it was easier and better for me, in fact, to just draft one single report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the binder I believe that you have to -- it's marked -- it's 65 ter number 7415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you speak closer to the microphone. The interpreters have a hard time hearing your voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document 65 ter number 7415?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it's this report of mine, if I'm not mistaken, if I can see the numbers correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it's in your binder, and it comes after the number 7415?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I got it, I got it. [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the document. This is the report that I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your report, specifically in section 2, do you describe the evolution of the directorate for areas outside areas of special state concern, the evolution from that entity -- the evolution of the ODPR into your current employers and organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there, throughout the years and throughout the transitions that you describe in section 2, was there continuity as far as the transfer of records, data and archives from one entity to the next?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact, that organisation, which was initially the governmental Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees, fully took over the database and the entire archives of the previous office. With those archives and the database, it had competence for certain fields of activity; and there's a department in one ministry and there's the structure of the ministry's change would become part of another ministry, that it continued to deal with those activities that concerned refugees. And refugees is a subject dealt with in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there also continuity in personnel from one entity to the next?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was continuity of personnel, naturally. Since we're talking about a governmental body, some people left that system, that body, but a significant number stayed on in that department from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for how long have you been with the department in the field of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Since 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to page 1 of your report, does that describe -- does that give us an overview of your responsibilities within the ODPR over the years?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were asked to prepare the joint report that you submitted for the Seselj case and the Stanisic/Simatovic case, were you asked to do that in your capacity as director?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was asked to do that before. Or, rather, the government designated me in accordance with the Prosecution request for me to testify in this case, and in this way I was to prepare this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the report was to deal with the subject of expelled persons from the area of Croatia that had been affected by the war from 1991 until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does your report cover any other geographical area outside of the Republic -- the former Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In part of the report, I address the issue of refugees from Serbia. This was in accordance with the Prosecution request, since this department or administration that I work in, the ODPR, among other things took care of refugees from neighbouring countries as well for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you define for the Trial Chamber, please, the term "displaced persons," as compared to "refugees"?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: When defining these terms, one took over the definitions used for refugees in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. It has to do with the status of refugees and with the relevant protocols. So there is a difference that has to be made, a distinction. When you talk about displaced persons, one is referring to internally-displaced persons who remain within the borders of the state of which they are citizen, so in fact they had to leave their place of residence and move to another place. But when the term "refugees" is used, then we are talking about people who, for the very same reasons, namely, threats to their lives, left the state of which they are citizens. And when we talk about refugees in Croatia, we are talking about people who have come from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, on the whole, at least when we're talking about registered refugees. According to our legal provisions, refugees are also considered to be people who left Croatia and moved to other countries; for example, they spent some time in Germany, and having returned -- they had some kind of refugee status over there, but having returned, they had the right to have the status of returnees, and that included expelled persons when they returned to their homes. In such cases, they would gain the status of returnees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly go over the structure of the report. Directing your attention to section 6 of the report, does that section describe the data source used in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And section 7 describes -- does that describe the data collection methodology used in the report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sections 9 through 12, do those sections detail the data, statistics and analysis on displaced persons within the former occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to section 10 of your report. I believe in meeting yesterday, you made a correction to a date that appeared there.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Any correction introduced from the preparation session, from the proofing, should have been provided to me in written form. Nothing was done in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, was Mr. Seselj notified that a date was going to be amended in the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's less -- the date is correct in another part of the report. The correction is with respect to one section of the report. We finished proofing yesterday at around 5.00, and it made sense to do it orally today in court, and it's not a substantial change. The change is to be consistent with another part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. If it's just a simple typo, please tell us what it is. What page is it on?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In e-court, it will be page 27, and in your binder, it will be marked page 26 of 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if I could direct your attention to the second paragraph of section 10, specifically to the second sentence that begins: "On 1st August 1994 ..." Is that date correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Should it read "1994"?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that sentence appears somewhere at the beginning of the report, and it's quite clear that we're talking about the year 1991. This is quite simply a typo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay, let me see if I can understand. The second sentence in the second paragraph in section 10 currently reads, in English: "On 1st August 1994 ..." Is that year correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No. It should say "1991."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention, and for the Trial Chamber it would read page 2 of 47 in your binder, in e-court it would be page 3 in the English version, the top of that page reads: "From 9.683 persons on 1st August 1991 ..." Is that what you mean when you say in another part of the report it appears correctly, the date?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the final section in your report, section 13, does that section describe the data pertaining to refugees from Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your report, you refer to 11 tables; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And those tables are attached and incorporated in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect -- setting aside table 1 for now, but for tables 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11, where did the data come from with respect to those tables?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: As far as tables 2, 3 and 4, these documents are original documents. It also concerns 5 and 6. These are original documents of the ODPR from the period referred to in the tables. So these are original documents. As far as 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 are concerned, well, similarly these are tables that were made by extracting data from the ODPR database. This was done on the basis of information or records that are kept in an electronic form on refugees in the Republic of Croatia from 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, going back to table 1, where did the data for that table come from?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The main data was obtained from the State Institute for Statistics in Croatia. It was in accordance or on the basis of the census of 1991, but it was compiled in a way to reflect the current territorial and administrative structure of the Republic of Croatia. So it was done on the basis of the towns, municipalities and counties that are now in the Republic of Croatia, and it relates exclusively to areas that were occupied or directly affected by the war, up until 1995, or 1998 if we're talking about Croatian Podunavlje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described where the underlying data came from. Who actually created the table, itself?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I created it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you independent in creating this report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you've previously described that the report details the methodology that you used in its creation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the results are based on -- with respect to the tables 2 through 11 are based on the official records kept by your employer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution moves for the admission of 65 ter number 7415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall determine the matter at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For ease of reference, would the Court like to assign an MFI number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that might be a good idea. Mr. Registrar, an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be marked for identification as Exhibit number P632. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, your -- in section 1 of your report, you describe your professional responsibilities. Could you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I finished primary and secondary school in Split, and received university education in Zagreb at the School of Philosophy, majoring in Sociology. So I'm, in fact, a sociologist. I am still at post-graduate studies at the School of Political Science of the University of Zagreb. According to the Bologna agreement, it's the equivalent of a Master degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, I will be asking for the English page 51 and the B/C/S page 34 of MFI P632 in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could now talk about tables 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 in general terms. The ODPR data depicted in those tables 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, from what time period does that data come from?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: These tables are from 1992. That is the time indicated on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said "1992"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in what months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The first table and the second and the third tables are for March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In March 1992, was there a formal registration of displaced persons within the then Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Not yet. The first formal registration was done in April 1992. At that time, people who were coming as displaced persons would report to the competent regional offices, of which there had been 16 by that time in the Republic of Croatia, and they reported to centres for social welfare that exist in all large cities and municipalities in Croatia. There were more than a hundred of them. They registered there, and they received a special ID for displaced persons. And thus this data was statistically collected through regional offices into the Zagreb office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what you just described was the situation that existed before April of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if we now look at table 2, English page 51, B/C/S page 34, could you tell us what that first table represents?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The first table represents the number of displaced persons as of that date in the Republic of Croatia, broken down by the places where they were accommodated in the Republic of Croatia. Of course, these are only major urban centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you give us the total number of those displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: 335.792 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to the second table of -- on that same page, is there also an illustration of the numbers of refugees from Croatia who were accommodated in other countries?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the total number is 125.381. This information was collected in contacts with other states and with the assistance of the UNHCR. In fact, primarily the UNHCR and contacts with other states where refugees from Croatia were received and accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The formal registration process that you describe as beginning in April of 1992, was that data put in an electronic database at that time in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When was data pertaining to displaced persons and refugees put in electronic format?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In 1994, after re-registration of both displaced persons and refugees. This was another -- after this first attempt at registration, we tried to put data into an electronic database, but it turned out to be impossible because we had not enough equipment and inadequate technology to do that job. It was necessary, first of all, to put information collected in the field into the database. And in that first attempt some of the data was put in electronic form, some was not, so it didn't work the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a few technical questions for you. The first chart or table, we have 326.012 individuals that were expelled or displaced. Under that figure, we have a figure of 9.780 individuals that were not registered, and it said "Estimate" in the chart. How could you estimate that, because these people were not registered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these 326.000 is the number of persons registered, but at that time, unfortunately, there were people who were not registered. And on the basis of information available at that time from the field, it was estimated that the percentage of the unregistered was at least 3 per cent, and that's the basis for this estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 9.780 is a figure that was just given as an estimate with the 3 per cent rule. In total, 335.782. Second chart, it deals with refugees that found themselves in Croatia and went to other countries. So I guess that in this overall figure, we may find people who were, for instance, registered in Dubrovnik and went to Germany. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, no. Really not at that time, because the Office for Displaced Persons that started issuing displaced persons IDs was established only at the end of 1991. You have to understand that at that time, displaced persons were flowing in by the thousands per day, and it was impossible to register them all at the same time at the end of 1991. The people reflected here were simply in one place, somewhere else, and then went to foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we could add the figures from chart 1 to chart 2 and we would have an overall figure of 460.000 persons. Do you agree with that figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How is it that among the countries, we do not find Serbia? Aren't there any refugees that went to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In another report that we will come to later, numbers 3 and 4, reference is made also to refugees who left for Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing strikes me. We have 55.000 persons for Germany; in other words, the German Federal Republic had opened its borders widely to refugees. Also in Hungary, because there we find 45.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was precisely the case at that time, and that number of refugees remained stable in Germany for quite a long time. They gave those people temporary refugee status and protection, and most of those people were in Germany until 1994, when an agreement was signed between Croatia and Germany on the return of refugees. And after that, systematically, people started to come back. And the number of refugees even increased in Germany later with the arrival of refugees from Bosnia and Croatia. The number reflected here are only refugees from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you account for the fact that Switzerland, which is the country with the status of refugees, we only have 164 people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the official figure at the time. At the beginning, that's what Switzerland had. Of course, later the number increased significantly, but the Swiss, obviously like other states, did not want to put forward estimates. The numbers for other states were mainly estimates, estimates either of the state's, such as Switzerland, or of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described the re-registration that occurred in 1994, which was also put into an electronic database. Was there another registration that followed the one in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In 1997, there was a re-registration, because in the meantime some changes had occurred in the ranks of the refugees and displaced persons, because some had returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if I could now have table 9, which is the English page 79 and the B/C/S page 65, please -- excuse me. Actually, if we could have table 7, the English at page 77 and the B/C/S at page 60. And it's quite a sprawling sheet. What I'd like to focus on is the portion that says: "County, Vukovar-Srem," and then the portion that says: "VS county, town of Vukovar." So it's on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you have that in your binder? It might be easier for you to see. It's in your binder?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that one, it's called "Statistics of Expelled Persons," is that correct, that table?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, after the re-registration process, was there another number that was developed for total displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was that number?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: After those several registration drives, we reached the number of refugees expressed in this table. That's 220.338 displaced persons, and they were displaced from the then occupied areas in Croatia in 1995, and displaced persons who came from areas adjacent to separation lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: According to your statistics and data, when were most of those people displaced?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: From the statistics, we see clearly that most of those people had been displaced in that period up to the end of 1991; that is, from the summer until the end of 1991. This number, reflecting the persons who were displaced from 1991 to 1995. And if we're talking about Podunavlje, then through 1998, that is the peaceful reintegration of the Podunavlje region, those people were displaced for seven years. At the time that we mentioned in earlier statistics dating back to 1992, the number of displaced persons is much higher, because at that time the population from major cities exposed to attacks also left their homes and left for other areas of Croatia, seeking safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in looking at this chart, the number of displaced persons in the Vukovar-Srem county?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The Vukovar-Srem county is divided into two spaces because of different dates of displacement taken as criteria here. The total number for the Vukovar-Srem county is 32.470, plus there is a number strictly for Vukovar, 23.174. In looking at these numbers, we have to bear in mind that in the meantime, 1.357 children were born, if we're talking about Vukovar. And if we are -- county -- if we're talking about Vukovar county, the number of babies born was 2.250. And that's how we reached the total number of displaced persons for the Vukovar-Srem county. That's 23.174 plus 32.470.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Based on your analysis of the data that you had at your disposal, were you able to determine the predominant group that was displaced?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the largest group of refugees or displaced persons were expelled by that date. If we are talking about Vukovar town, that's the 18th November 1991. If we are talking about the rest of the Vukovar-Srem county, that is, settlements around Vukovar, they were displaced by 20th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us if most of these people were -- what ethnicity were they, the ones who were displaced?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The majority of displaced persons are Croats, as we can see from table 9, with a proviso that in this total number, 25.215 -- that is, 205.215 Croats, and in Vukovar town and Vukovar county, we have 29.770 Croats plus 21.235 if we are talking about the town of Vukovar. There are some Serbs among the displaced persons, that should not be forgotten, a total of 500 -- I'll try to calculate it now, 578 persons who were Serbs. The rest are members of other ethnic communities, ethnic minorities who lived in that area of Croatia. And precisely in that area of Croatia, there were a lot of ethnic minorities; Hungarians, Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a general question regarding these tables, especially their titles. Indeed, they say "Expelled Persons," so that would -- or whose departure or displacement would be motivated. Was it possible to determine whether these people were displaced because they'd been expelled or is it possible that somebody decided to leave voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were people who were literally expelled. They left their homes because of bombing, shelling, or direct entry of the military units of the JNA, or paramilitary units. So these people had to leave their homes. In some cases, like the notorious case of Vukovar, but also Ilok and some other places, several localities found themselves under siege, in complete encirclement, and these people were simply forced to leave. The army put them on buses, at least some of them, and deported them from their towns and villages; and in many cases people simply ran from the military units that were entering their places, and they had to leave their homes. Now, these people referred to here are expelled persons who found shelter and accommodation in other areas of Croatia that were not occupied at the time, and they were under the control of the legitimate authorities of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you would agree with me in saying that in these tables, you are using a very broad concept of expellees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think it is a very broad definition of expulsion that I'm using, because the concept of expulsion coincides with the very substance of refugee status, as defined in the conventions. These are people who left their homes, fearing for their lives, under direct threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one objection, Mr. President. I believe the Prosecution should, at least by the next break, get us the definition of "refugees" and the definition of "deported persons" from the Geneva Conventions, because through this report the Prosecution is offering us definitions from the Croatian legislation, and that's why we are confused between the terms "refugee" and "deported" or "expelled."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the reason for Judge Lattanzi's questions. Of course, if we ask questions, you must understand that we have legal interrogations. I don't think you have more than ten minutes left, so please come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The figures that you have just described, in your opinion, do they capture all the persons who would fall under the definition of displaced persons, when we're talking about the former Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: These figures, since this is information contained in our database, kept electronically from 1994 onwards, capture persons who were expelled at that time and remained refugees for a long time, at least from 1991 to 1995, or alternatively 1998. However, this database does not contain persons who were refugees from 1991 to 1994, April 1994, when this registration drive occurred, and who in the meantime either left Croatia for third states and did not return, but stayed in third countries, that is, they passed through Croatia in transit, and there was a certain number of persons who, for personal reasons best known to them, did not register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be more specific? While these are impressive figures, we do not intend to dispute them as to their volumes, but could you give a precise answer to this hypothetical question? Let us imagine that we have a given village which is the target of a military JNA offensive. Let us imagine that the inhabitants of that village leave it because they're being shot at. The people leaving the village, are they regarded by you as expelled people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, very well. Let's assume that 40 kilometres away from that village, we have another village, and in that village they find out that in the first village, there was an attack by the JNA, and that in another village 30 kilometres away from there, people are leaving their homes. This second group of people, would you consider them as expellees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991, these people were also considered -- or, rather, such people were also considered to be refugees. But our first decrees that precisely defined who could be considered to be a refugee, well, these decrees were adopted in 1991 and subsequently in 1992. In 1992, the definition was that people from places such as Osijek, which had been shelled at the time -- we're not talking about a neighbouring village, but a major town that was directly shelled, and many people, especially women with their children, left that place, well, at that time the definition was those people couldn't be granted the status of refugees, since their homes had not been damaged and it was possible for them to return there. So in 1992, according to the rules in Croatia, only people who could not return to their homes were considered to be refugees, because their place of residence, their towns and villages, were totally occupied and under the control of Serbian units or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do not try to confuse matters, my question was very specific. I gave you a very specific case, and I'm not asking you to tell us about various decrees or laws. I'm asking you whether -- if we have a village 40 kilometres away from the first village, where people start leaving their home, although the JNA is nowhere to be found, are the people that are leaving the second village considered as refugees, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just for that reason, not at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the case in which the JNA does not go to that second village because that village is of no interest to the JNA? What about the village inhabitants who go and have themselves registered in Zagreb; do you consider them as displaced persons or as expellees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're not included in this figure of 220.330 refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they can't be included because they are able to return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we take the break and before the beginning of the cross-examination by Mr. Seselj, I have a number of technical questions to put to the witness. Witness, I had a look at your CV, and I saw that you started your professional life as a journalist. You were working for the Hina News Agency. What was your area of specialty as a journalist? Did you cover politics, sports, environmental matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Internal politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, internal politics. But could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was a fairly young journalist, just starting my career in Zagreb; and on the whole I covered events in Zagreb in 1992 up until the end of 1993. That's when I worked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "events," do you mean by that political events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, various press conferences, meetings, visits of foreign politicians coming to Zagreb. Hina is an agency that covers a lot of events that occur in Zagreb. Some other newspapers wouldn't cover such events, for example. So it's only involved in news. It's not involved in writing other kinds of articles and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the Hina News Agency a news agency that was completely independent from the political authorities or was it under their control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a state agency or it is a state agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was under the control of the state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because it's a state agency, yes. But the question as to whether something is a state organisation or not, well, I don't think that has anything to do with the independence of the agency, as an agency involved in the media; but there's no doubt about the fact that it's owned by the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Fine. At the very beginning of your testimony, I asked you a question about Serb displaced persons; in other words, Croatian nationals belonging to the Serb ethnicity. In your view, how many people of that category left their home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, it's very difficult. I'll give you my opinion here. I can tell you about things that I'm familiar with. I can present some facts to you with regard to what I know about refugees from Croatia, refugees of Serbian ethnicity who left the Republic of Croatia. Well, unfortunately, we don't have precise information or records on this matter, records on how many refugees there are of Serbian ethnicity, and the majority of them in Serbia and a few of them in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even a lower number in Montenegro. But with regard to this matter, we never had very precise information or records. International organisations and part of the Serbian public, at various periods of time, had certain assessments. Unfortunately, we never exchanged information for refugees who were from Croatia, but fled to Serbia; so we could never determine how many people were actually concerned. What we do know is some people in the meantime returned to the Republic of Croatia, and they were registered with us, and we have files for them. This concerns almost 127.000 people at this point in time. So the administration that I work in also deals with the return of Serbs to the Republic of Croatia, among other things, and they keep records on people who register with us as returnees. As far as the information we currently have, in Serbia there are currently about 70.000 refugees from Croatia. Assessments of international organisations, the estimates of these organisations, are more or less the same, the figure is more or less the same, but it's not very precise. And I really can't say much about these figures, because we're only talking about estimates here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now move on to another topic, where you may help us understand a better what it's all about. A number of witnesses came here to testify about exchanges of apartments. At the time, some of them, Serbs, lived in Croatia, and they were asked to go away and to exchange their apartments with Croats who at the time were living in Serbian areas. So we had witnesses here tell us about this, and they showed us contracts related to exchanges of apartments. We have received a number of evidence in that respect. You are dealing with statistics, with data, and I would like to know whether, according to you, these people who exchanged their apartments were recorded in the statistics, were they considered as displaced persons or refugees? But before you answer my question, another question. Were you aware of such things going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware of the fact that such things were done. However, many cases had to do with refugees who came to Croatia from Serbia. To be more precise, many people from Vojvodina came to Croatia in this manner. They exchanged their property for property that belonged to people who had decided to leave Croatia, people of Serbian ethnicity. The same thing occurred with refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina at a later date. Houses were exchanged not just with people from Vojvodina but also with people from Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, as far as people from Vojvodina themselves are concerned, some of these people were registered in our offices as refugees because they were from a different state, they came from a different state to the Republic of Croatia. However, some of these people who exchanged their houses didn't register as refugees with us. They did not have the need, since they had managed to exchange their property, they had a place to stay; and so some of these people didn't feel the need to register as refugees in order to obtain certain benefits and advantages; for example, accommodation, food, social security, because they also obtained Croatian nationality very rapidly, because we're talking about the Croats, the Croatian national minority that lived in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you've said is extremely relevant. I believe I understand that Croats from Vojvodina exchanged their property with Serbs who were in Croatia, and that these people decided that they did not need to register as refugees because they saw themselves as being Croats; and they did not request any type of help or benefits. Were there many such cases, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were quite a few such people, but I couldn't provide you with a precise figure with regard to the number of people we have registered as refugees. Well, we can't say whether this concerned everyone or just some of them, but we have registered refugees from Vojvodina, we have 5.131 refugees from Vojvodina. As far as 3.377 of these refugees are concerned, we have information according to which they are of Croatian ethnicity. However, we don't have any information for about 1.511 individuals who initially did not register as refugees; but as of 2002, when Croatia made this possible, they asked for our assistance in finding accommodation for them, so some of the people who arrived by exchanging their property did not register as refugees because at the time they did not need any assistance when it came to accommodation, but later on they did report to us. Those who felt the immediate need at the time, on the whole, registered as refugees. I think we're dealing more with certain personal reasons and not with other reasons for which someone decided to register as a refugee or not to do that. This was thought to be humanitarian aid, a matter of humanitarian aid if you registered as a refugee. It was only later that things changed, when people understood that it also had a lot to do with requests for renovating your home, when you returned to your home, if you returned to your home, or if you had requests for accommodation if you didn't have a home to return to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You are a high-ranking civil servant of the Republic of Croatia. As such, we can consider that you are aware of what's going on now. To your knowledge, are there any disputes between people who at the time exchanged their property, but then later realised that the exchange was not fair because the property they received in the exchange was worth less than the one they had let go? So has your government been seized of such disputes? Are there trials or proceedings going on in that respect, or is it something that you have no information about? I'm asking you the question, because we had witnesses here tell us that when it came to the exchange, they did not receive what they gave. So my question is very straightforward. Are you aware of cases of people who exchanged their property at the time and are now asking for damage or who have started legal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't keep records about such cases. Recently, I haven't heard anything about any individual cases. However, since this isn't the responsibility of my ministry, I don't have to be aware of such cases; but I have to admit that recently I haven't heard anything about such cases. But I have heard that legal proceedings have been instituted for such reasons. I don't know what numbers we're dealing with here, but I do know that there were such cases when it comes to exchanges of property with Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if you're asking me to provide you with figures, I really couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One very last question. Rest assured, it is actually my very last question, and it relates to these people who exchange their property and who came from Vojvodina to Zagreb or the surrounding areas. To your knowledge in the ensuing years or even today, do any of these people go back to Vojvodina or is everybody very pleased with their current situation? Has everybody decided to stay put? And if some people decide to go back where they came from, do you have any idea how many they are, do you have a percentage to give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any of these people returning to their homes. As far as I know, these people did not return to their homes. Quite the contrary. Some family members who came to Croatia would later bring other family members who had perhaps remained in Serbia to Croatia, so, in fact, most of the family members remained in Croatia and live in Croatia. But as to how satisfied they are or not, well, that's something you should ask them about. But what everyone knows with regard to refugees and international investigations has also demonstrated this, and this doesn't just concern Croatian refugees in Croatia, but also Serbians in Serbia, after many years spent abroad as a refugee, the family situation changes and then people decide whether to return or not on that basis. It has nothing to do with how happy they are or not. Parents, well, that's one matter. Children, that's another matter. Elderly grandparents is another matter again. We're talking about living individuals here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My fellow Judges may have some questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Radic, the report that you have made, as I have understood it, mostly deals with the registration of persons who moved from various areas to other areas, but the question I have to you is if you have any information about how this was organised in practical terms. And I'm asking because if you have hundreds of thousands of people moving in one direction or in several directions and almost as many people moving in the other direction, that is, in and of itself, an enormous logistical task, and I would have thought that it would require a very high degree of organisation. And my question to you is: Do you know how this was organised in practical terms? I mean, how would a family from one place, who felt compelled to leave their home and go to -- let's say they would move from, just as an example, from Vukovar to Zagreb. How would they be able to find a vacant home there without being assisted by private organisations, or by government bodies, or by somebody else? It would seem to be that there would have to be some sort of organisation, either private or government- sponsored, to put some degree of order and organisation into all of this. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think that this has been fairly well explained in my report. In fact, at the time the organisation that first started taking care of displaced persons and refugees was the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare. That ministry deals with such matters, matters of social welfare, and in Croatia, in most towns and municipalities, it has social welfare centres which were part of the ministry at the time. So these were their field offices. They would deal with family matters, with children who had special needs, with disabled persons, people who were socially at risk, and they had their principles. So at the time, there was the Croatian Red Cross. It still exists. And in many towns, in many municipalities in the Republic of Croatia, the Red Cross had its own offices and its own staff members. When all these are taken together, the ministry, within which that office for displaced persons and refugees was first established at the very end of 1991, and the independent governmental body – the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees - they, in fact, organised the reception of individuals in the free areas of the Republic of Croatia. I don't want to present you with a false picture, but how did things unfold? Well, in certain cases people simply fled from their homes, carrying bags with them and nothing else. This happened on a number of cases. People from Drnis became expelled persons in this way. Many people from Lika became expelled persons in this way. This also concerns areas around Slunja. Immediately prior to the entry of military units after intense shelling had occurred, these people simply fled from their homes. In many cases, people simply fled from their villages, others -- some had transport, others had nothing. And there were people who would receive them at certain places. It was quite complicated. In the case of Vukovar or Ilok, people were transported out in buses. They were bussed out in Vukovar, and the date concerned is the 18th of November. Well, that's the anniversary when the JNA and paramilitary units entered Vukovar and captured the remaining population there. They had been assembled at several points, and on the following day the civilians, the women, children and the elderly, were put into buses and transported through Novi Sad and Bosnia to Croatia, via Slavonski Brod, Djakovo and Zagreb. People knew that the buses were arriving, so some of these people were put up in sports halls at the time. The Red Cross naturally provided these people with food. So there was a civilian headquarters that organised the reception of such people. These were the most difficult tasks, when such huge groups of people arrived as was the case with Vukovar or Ilok. So some people from Vukovar were received in Slavonski Brod, some in Djakovo, and most of them in Zagreb. Most of them ended up in Zagreb. On the first day, at around 9.00, about 3.000 people from Vukovar were received in Zagreb, and they were provided with accommodation at the premises -- on the premises of the fair. There were also hotels in Zagreb, five-star or four-star hotels, that we used to provide these people with accommodation, too. At the time, we didn't have any settlements for refugees, so they were first provided with accommodation at the seaside, on the coast. If they were refugees, they would be first gathered in sports halls, in large buildings, schools. Usually they were assembled in schools, and then they were sent on to other places. Naturally, many people found accommodation with relatives of theirs, and later they asked for the state to assist them and to provide them with accommodation elsewhere. So they would assemble in these large centres, and we would send them on. At the time, all the hotels on the Adriatic coast were used to provide these refugees with accommodation. That was the case for a long time. So many of the well-known hotels we used for such purposes. To present you with a vivid description, about 11.000 refugees were provided with accommodation in Dubrovnik hotels, or, rather, let's be more precise. 11.000 expelled persons were provided with accommodations there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll have to take the break now, but my next question to you would be -- and I will give the question to you now so you can consider your answer in the break. The -- from the point in time when the refugees had arrived and had been accommodated in these hotels and schools and places, how then would the authorities or the institutions who assisted these refugees know about vacant homes, because there must have been then a registration of, say, Serbs who left Zagreb to return to Serbia, so that the authorities knew that the authorities in Croatia would know which houses would be available for the refugees from Vojvodina or other parts. And my second question to that is: Do you know if there was any cooperation between Croatian authorities and Serbian authorities to organise this? These are the two questions that I would like you to consider. Let's have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had a break, Witness. Can you now answer the questions put by Judge Harhoff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in response to your first question, where you asked, in fact, how the authorities were aware of houses that were available to refugees from Vojvodina and other areas, to displaced persons, I'll try to be a bit more precise. As far as the ODPR is concerned, the office which was in charge of accommodating displaced persons and refugees and expelled persons at the time, the ODPR, as the competent agency of the Republic of Croatia, did not have lists at that time. We're talking about 1991 to 1995. It did not have a list of vacant houses and flats where they could put up displaced persons. We used exclusively facilities for organised accommodation. At that time, that included all the hotel-type facilities, workers' prefab houses, and then we proceeded with building dedicated accommodation. Already in 1993 and 1994, we started building such accommodation near Osijek, with the assistance of the German government, also near Karlovac and Vinkovci, and each of these buildings had a capacity of accommodating 3.000 persons. We did not put people up in private accommodation. If displaced persons went to private accommodation, it was usually with family, with friends, who would let them use a house or a flat they had or would simply receive them as guests. Later on, it turned out that some people could not go on staying in such private accommodation and had to turn to something more organised. As for houses and flats that were abandoned, one of the competences of our agency is accommodating displaced persons from Serbia, people who had tenants' rights to housing. I know that Croatian courts, based on Croatian legislation, in regard to people who had tenants' rights to housing, brought in verdicts that such housing rights were annulled if it was established that somebody did not live in a certain house or apartment for more than six months. Such flats and houses existed. However, at that time it was municipalities and towns that had the right to dispose of such housing, not the ODPR. So I cannot answer the question in what way some of the displaced persons were accommodated in such vacant housing. It is a well-known fact that as time went on, some of these people addressed themselves to us for assistance, and they received decisions on accommodation; but that did not happen in 1991. It happened in 1992 through 1995 that some displaced persons were accommodated in some of the abandoned, vacant housing. This thing that I'm describing, that we put up displaced persons in an organised way in such housing, that was later, closer to the Operation Storm. But in the period I was talking about, we could only put up people in organised accommodation, and we did not have any flats at our disposal. As for your second question, whether at that time there was cooperation between Croatia and Serbia, it simply did not exist at that time. There was no cooperation whatsoever regarding the accommodation of displaced people. The war was simply going on. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard some of the witnesses in this trial, who came to testify earlier, that there was, on the Serb side, a private organisation called Lasta, and that they were able to provide some assistance, on the Serbian side, to refugees who came to Serbia, I think. So what I was curious to know was that if there were -- if you know of the existence of any similar private organisations on the Croatian side who would be able to assist in this exchange of property. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. That must have been some private agency or agencies in the area concerning real estate sale and purchase. That did not fall within the jurisdiction of the ODPR. Everything that concerns trade and economy, that is within the sphere of private business. We, as a state institution, did not deal with that. People found each other in some private contacts. We don't know anything about it. We don't know if there is an organisation who was involved. Today, we have a state agency that purchases real estate on behalf of the state in Croatia, but it was established only in 1997, during the peaceful reintegration of Croatian Podunavlje region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may begin with the cross-examination. You were granted one hour and 30 minutes by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, do you believe yourself to be an expert?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In this area that I'm dealing with, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you appear anywhere before as an expert in this area?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do others in Croatia believe you to be an expert?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did you appear as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: At many international conferences, seminars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an expert in the area of displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, for what happened in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You said you were designated by the Croatian government to make a report and testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that means that the Prosecution did not contact you directly; they contacted the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP asked the Croatian government, and the Croatian government designated you, trusting that you will do that job the best?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you did it on the orders of your government, within your working hours?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Whether it was within my working hours, I don't know, if you believe working hours to be 10 or 12 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I sometimes worked 16 hours a day. Anyway, you may have done overtime, but you did it in your workplace?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you had to take some of it home?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you had to engage government officials to help you with the data?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: To a smaller extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you are an expert of the Croatian government, lent to the Croatian -- to the OTP to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you are also to testify in the Simatovic and Stanisic case, which is in preparation?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did anyone explain to you what it means to be an expert witness before a court? Did they give you some basic instructions in principle, because you have never appeared in court before?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I have never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were a government expert who appeared at international conferences and defended the interests of your government on this issue or, rather, represented the interests?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anyone instruct you what it means to be a forensic expert?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I was instructed by the OTP, who asked me to do certain things, and I believe I wrote those things in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have read your report, although I received it, together with the background material, only last Friday. I read it very conscientiously. Don't worry, we'll discuss it all. These are questions in principle. I am interested in your status here. Did anyone tell you that you are representing the interests of the Croatian government here or that you have to testify in an unbiased way, even at the detriment of the interests of the Croatian government? Did anyone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the concept of expert or professional, that implies precisely what you're saying; namely, that one must be impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, then, did you not take the trouble to prove that you are impartial in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'll show what I mean. Did anyone communicate to you that at first the Prosecution planned to use Colonel Ivan Grujic as the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they didn't tell you that at all?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is in the official papers here, it is evident that the Prosecution replaced Ivan Grujic because he was compromised, and two other persons were used to replace him, Ms. Visnja Bilic and you?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I was not informed by the Prosecution of that, but I know that Mr. Grujic covered this area in some other prior cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But if they had told you that Ivan Grujic had been disqualified for such-and-such a reason, and you are called to testify instead of him, what would have been your response?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I was not designated to testify on this issue either by Mr. Grujic or by the Prosecution, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: By the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: -- by the Croatian government for which I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your answer is very satisfactory to me. But do you know Mr. Ivan Grujic personally?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He is a brigadier general now, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know why he was disqualified?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that Ivan Grujic used to be the head of the war branch office of the State Security Service in Osijek in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in 2001, Ivan Grujic testified in the investigation in the Glavas case concerning the killing of Serb civilians in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I did not follow the news that much, not sufficiently to know all that happened there. It concerns no segment of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, you are a high-ranking civil servant, an employee of the government, if you wish. You are well educated. You have a university degree. You majored in Sociology. You are doing post-graduate studies. I suppose you watch television, listen to the radio and read newspapers.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Of course I watch television, of course I listen to the radio and read newspapers, but believe me, there is so much information and news in all the mass media that you can't know it all. I did not know this particular thing. I may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Branimir Glavas is?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Croatian general, an MP in the Croatian Parliament, a prominent politician. He even had his own party. He was an important man for the regime at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's now on trial; you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's on trial for war crimes against Serb civilians in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's the indictment against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what he is being tried for. I'm not prejudging the decision of the Court, because he had been acquitted for certain things before. There is a certain [indiscernible] case also. You know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Only from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, same here. My associates found certain material on the internet concerning Ivan Grujic earlier, because I didn't have time to prepare specially for you and I did not explore your CV; but I believe there are no compromising things, as there are for Ivan Grujic.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I wouldn't have found any, would I? I have here the Nacional Weekly and then I have the Feral tribune newspaper. Ivan Grujic was a key witness in the Glavas case, and in 2001, in the process, he incriminated Glavas very heavily. And then suddenly in 2006, he withdrew all his incriminations against Glavas as head of the state security in Osijek. He knew about all of Glavas' crimes. Before the Investigating Judge, he incriminated him seriously, and then he withdrew all that because there turned out evidence that Ivan Grujic was involved in the murder of Reihl Kir. And even though Grujic gave an interview to Robert Bajrusi of the Nacional Weekly, he refused to talk about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can only thank you for all this information. I had no such details. I didn't know at all that Mr. Grujic was involved in that case. I may have read something in the Nacional Weekly, but I must say I didn't pay much attention to that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respectfully request some clarification from Mr. Seselj regarding the relevance of the information about Mr. Grujic in the context of this witness's expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, where is the relevance? Why is it relevant to know that Mr. Grujic, who was supposed to be a Prosecution expert, was withdrawn, to be replaced by another two individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm checking the expert's credibility, first of all. I'm doing this with considerable success. That would be my subjective assessment. The Prosecution should explain to you why they did not ask for an independent witness perhaps from the International Red Cross, who would draft a report on the expelled and displaced persons in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that would include the territory of Croatia. Instead of doing this, the Prosecution contacted the Croatian government, and the Croatian government designates Ms. Radic to draft an expert report. I think this is an unheard-of scandal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, in your country, as in mine, this kind of situation would not happen, because experts are independent persons appointed by judges. But this is a type of Anglo-Saxon proceedings in which each party calls their own experts. The case law established by the Appeals Chamber is that such experts can be independent. Well, that's what the Appeals Chamber says. So you, when you call your own experts, that will be the same. The Prosecutor could say that your expert is not independent. This is an endless topic for discussion. It would have been better if the experts had been appointed by the Trial Chamber, following motions by parties, and this sort of situation would not have cropped up. But we have Rules establishing these proceedings, so the Prosecution can choose their own expert, including their own staff members, and can ask a government to send their representatives. That's it. You may have your own view upon it, but that's allowed by the Rules. Only following the testimony of the witness and following cross-examination, the Trial Chamber will decide whether the report should be admitted or not. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are quite right. However, something new cropped up here. We're not talking about a Prosecution expert, but about an expert representing the Croatian government, and the Prosecution and the Croatian government have joined forces here against me. So far, we have heard five experts that work for the Prosecution, staff members of the Prosecution, and now we have experts sent by the Croatian government. The Prosecution didn't find them and then assign them tasks, but the Prosecution told the government in Croatia, "We need such and stuff a thing," and then the Croatian government acted accordingly. So this is something new with regard to the practice to date. And I had to draw your attention to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, you probably know who Reihl Kir was.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was the head of the police in Osijek, of German nationality, but a local German, so he was of German ethnic origin. And Reihl Kir wanted the Serbs and the Croats to find a peaceful solution to the crisis in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. He wanted to make sure that there were no incidents, there was no killing, no shooting. Have I described him correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know that much about Reihl Kir, so I really couldn't say whether I agree with you or not. This isn't my area. All I know about Reihl Kir is from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. But you must know that as the head of the Osijek police, Reihl Kir was killed by the Croats in 1991. You must be aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I really am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I'm not here to discuss those events, because I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, you're here to answer my questions, and I'm not putting any insulting questions to you; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. And I'll continue in this way. But you must answer all my questions, and if there's something you don't know, just say so, and we'll move on. Since you worked as a journalist in Zagreb in 1992 and you worked for a state agency as a journalist, were you aware of the fact that the Croatian government, from 1991 to 1995, used the premises of the Zagreb Fair or Velesajam as a camp where they detained civilians, and several thousand Zagrebian Serbs passed through that camp; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you're a sociology graduate, do you know who Professor Zarko Puhovski is?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
