utterances.text: Yes. He was one of my professors at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's a very distinguished professor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was also the president of the Croatian Helsinki Committee?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he made a documentary film about the camp at the Zagreb Trade Fair. You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. We won't linger on that theme if you're not aware of it. When you were drafting this report, did you consult literature on expulsion and deportation of Serbs in Croatia from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go into such documents for this report, because the subject of my report was the expulsion of individuals from an area about which I have clear information. With regard to the Serbs, we have information about the return of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not about the departure of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not about the departure of Serbs, because in this area or these areas, areas in Croatia that were occupied, they were called "Krajina" at the time, they were under the supervision of UNPROFOR and they weren't part of the legal structure of the government in Croatia, they weren't under the control of the government, so we weren't aware of what was happening in those areas. Later, when people started returning, and then they all started recounting their stories, we found out that quite a lot of people left those areas in the period from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about areas that were under the control of the Croatian government in Zagreb all the time, and from that area hundreds of thousands of Serbs were expelled. That's what I'm asking you about. Did you have a look at the literature about that subject, if you don't have any official information?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: We don't have any official information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who Professor Svetozar Livada is?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I've heard that name, but I'm not sure who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A professor at the Zagreb University. He's currently retired, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He has published a lot of books containing detailed information on the expulsion of Serbs from the territory of Croatia, territory that was constantly or continually under the control of the Croatian government. The Prosecution has his publications, his statements and so on, but you have no knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: There are a lot of books that have been published. They are based on various assessments as to how many Serbs left Croatia. What I can tell you about has to do with official information regarding how many people were living in the area that was occupied or the areas that were occupied at the time, how many people returned in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who occupied the areas?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: At the time, those areas were not part of the legal structure of the Republic of Croatia, and in 1991 that area was occupied by the JNA and by paramilitary units. And later on, they said their name was "Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can the JNA occupy parts of Yugoslavia, since the JNA was the regular Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: But the Republic of Croatia was an independent state at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In 1991. The 8th of October, 1991, is when a decision was issued by the Croatian Parliament according to which all legal links to the SFRY were being discontinued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who accepted this?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: It's the decision of the Croatian Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a functionary of the Croatian Parliament, you always say that those decisions are legal that I'm asking you. Who recognised this legal act as a valid one? No one.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: It was recognised to be valid subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Subsequently. But previously, the territory of the Serbian Krajina came under the protection of the United Nations, and then the independence of Croatia was recognised?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite correct. UNPROFOR was deployed up until May 1992, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They needed a little more time. But according to the Vance Plan -- well, the Vance Plan was accepted before Germany, the Vatican, and other European countries recognised the independence of Croatia; isn't that correct? First of all, the Vance Plan was accepted and then the independence of Croatia was recognised; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know when the Vance Plan was adopted. It's not my field of expertise, so I cannot address the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's such an important thing that every intellectual should know about it, especially you Croatian intellectuals should be aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's what you think, but as you can see, I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. So what can I do? There's nothing I can do for you. There's some terminologically confusion in your report. You refer to the Croatian law on the Status of Expelled Persons and Refugees. That's the name of the law?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you said that an expelled person is a person who left his place of residence in order to avoid threats to his life as a result of aggression, and this individual found a place of residence in another part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in terms of international law, is this an arbitrary definition of what an expelled person is?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, look, as far as that definition is concerned, the definition you find in the Geneva Conventions, well, I just want to say something. I'm not a professional lawyer, so I cannot discuss this subject as a lawyer, but I know certain things on the basis of experience, because this is a subject that has been discussed at length. Allow me to finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: According to the Geneva Convention, the definition of a refugee is quite broad. It refers to a real threat that an individual feels when leaving his or her state of origin. One leaves because one fears for one's life or one is being prosecuted, it's because of one's religious beliefs, one's gender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you about expelled persons.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: They are internally-displaced persons, in fact, and the UNHCR, as a UN organisation, has accepted this definition. This Geneva Convention that defines the status of a refugee, in the 1950s of the last century, well, given what happened -- has happened over the years, this definition was adapted to include war refugees, people who are refugees because of war, people who have crossed a border and they have left their country of origin and are therefore refugees; or we are dealing with people who are internally-displaced individuals, and they have remained in their states of origin. This is the case in many states to this very day. You've seen the news on the Congo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Refugees are people who are fleeing in the face of a real danger, a real threat; do we agree?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It could be a matter of war, a flood, an earthquake, political terror; it could be anything. A refugee flees in the face of danger, whereas an expelled person is a deported person, people who are ordered to leave. Because one threatened to use force, an order was issued, they were told: "Either you leave or we'll arrest you. Either you leave or we'll kill you. Either you leave voluntarily or we'll take you to the border ourselves." So expelled persons are deported persons; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, they are similarly described according to Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, you said something else here. You said that an expelled person is, in fact, a refugee within the territory of Croatia itself, this move from Krajina to other parts of Croatia. That's what you said. It doesn't really matter. So there's terminologically confusion here. In your opinion, an expelled person is someone who, for various reasons, left the territory of Serbian Krajina and moved to Croatia. Was it a matter of danger, was it actually a deported person? Well, for you, it doesn't matter, they are all expelled persons for you. And this gave rise to the terminologically confusion that you are guilty of. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I quite clearly stated what the definition was. I'll try and repeat that. That's all I can do. That is how an expelled person is defined according to Croatian law. These are individuals who have left territory affected by war in Croatia, and they have left their place of residence because they were fleeing in front -- in the face of danger, and they found shelter in other places in the Republic of Croatia. So they left these occupied areas, crisis-affected areas. But as for the manner in which they were deported, well, every man was different. It depended on the case. We're talking about a lot of people. They weren't all bussed out on the same day and then moved somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: People who were put onto buses and forcibly taken somewhere, well, such people are expelled or deported people. The people who fled from Knin because they felt that they were facing a real threat, well, they are not expelled persons, they are refugees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: We are dealing with a matter of linguistics that I believe may not be entirely clear to somebody who is a native English speaker. The word "prognanik" should properly be translated as "expellee." In Croatian legislation, we used the word "prognanik," "expellee" and we defined it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In such a way as to include refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In such a way as to include all the things you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. You wanted to create a terminologically confusion deliberately to muddle the substance. You are -- you are confusing refugees with deported people, and the people who are interpreting you into English really have a problem. I, for one, do not use English, and that language is disgusting to me, to be frank, but "refugee" is one thing and "expelled person" is another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do not make such attacks against various languages. It's completely irrelevant. Witness, we are dealing with very complex legal definitions. You are not a lawyer, so let's not waste any time. But the Croatian term you use in your report, if I understand properly, excuse my pronunciation, it's something that sounds like "prognanik." Is this the word used, as Mr. Seselj seems to be saying, is it the word used to describe refugees and displaced persons? Does the word "prognanik" cover all these situations or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It covers persons who have fled within the borders and remained within the borders of Croatia, on the condition that they left home to avoid a direct threat to their lives. That's what I said. But we have already defined it earlier. These are people who fled from those occupied areas or crisis areas and could not return to their homes for a long time. It's not for one day; it lasted for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And in your language, what word do you use to describe a refugee who went to Switzerland? You know, these 164 people who went to Switzerland, what word would you use in your language to describe those people?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: "Izbjeglica," "refugee," and as such they have been defined by the law. There is a legal provision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you spell the word for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I-Z-B-J-E-G-L-I-C-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this word covers refugees within the meaning of the Geneva Conventions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct, but the definition applied by the law is, in fact, adjusted. This adjusted definition speaks of war refugees. It refines the definition of war refugees. You said it yourself, I'm not a lawyer, and I'm certainly not an expert in international law dealing with refugees. I'm just saying what I know, and I can define the term as it is defined in the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, with respect to the definition given by your Croatian legislation, all the "izbjeglica" coming from the territories where there was fighting are considered to be expelled persons, something that sounds like "prognanik," am I right, did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, do you agree that you and I speak the same language?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The languages are similar. We understand each other very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We understand each other. Well, what is different in our languages is a new development, and you find it hard to find your way in these new changes in the Croatian language. I notice -- first I notice you said "izvjestaj" and then you said "izvjesce." Once, and we can hear it on the tape-recording, you said "sistem," and then you said the new Croatian "sustav." These are new differences.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that with certainty. Both "izvjestaj" and "izvjesce" are equally used in the Croatian language. I don't see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You Croats used words "izvjestaj" and "system," and a few years ago somebody instructed you to change it, and now you are using "izvjesce" and "sustav" in order to differentiate yourself from the Serbs. Here you gave a table -- an overview of population in areas of the Republic of Croatia that were occupied in 1991. Tell me, which international legal document or document of the Prosecution defines that the area of Serbian Krajina, from 1991 to 1995, is in fact an occupied Croatian area; do you know of any specific legal document?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know all the international legal documents that define it, but there were certain UN resolutions that talked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Occupation?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: And in addition, international forces of the UNPROFOR were deployed in those areas, areas that were occupied and affected by the war. The UNPROFOR was deployed there, so there was some kind of UN resolution defining which areas those were. Later on, so-called Pink zones were designated with demarcation lines, and in this table you see all these places enumerated according to the new administrative division of the Republic of Croatia, which is a bit different from the previous one. And these were later defined by Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, the United Nations officially called these areas of Serbian Krajina UNPAs, United Nations Protected Areas; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why didn't you use at least this neutral term, if you don't want to say "Serbian Krajina"? Why do you use the terms used by the Croatian state propaganda, saying "occupied areas" as if Krajina Serbs could have occupied it themselves?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I do not see there anything problematic, because I heard this term, "occupied area," in statements of the Prosecution. We did consider these areas to be occupied, because for fours years they were outside the control of the officially, legally-elected authorities in Zagreb. And I know some people who had been expelled from these areas, and I know that we were not able to return them to their homes for these particular reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, when the Republic of Croatia was internationally recognised as an independent state, the area of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or, rather, UNPA, was outside of the Zagreb government control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And under international law, when a newly-created state is recognised, it can only be recognised within the territory that its central authorities control. Did anyone inform you of that? You are an expert. An expert must know sociology, political science, economy, psychology, international law. No, nobody told you?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have to give you this answer: I know a few things on the topics you are mentioning. However, I'm not here to speak on these subjects; and I was not brought here, as an expert, to speak on topics of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're dealing with very complex legal matters, and the witness is not an expert in that field. I have a question for you; not a matter of substance, but at page 57, line 23, you said that: "When the Republic of Croatia was internationally recognised as an independent state," you seem to be implying that this did not imply the UNPA. Is this what you meant to say or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me? Under international law, this could not have included territories under the protection of the United Nations, because according to the Vance Plan, those territories came under UN protection so that negotiations may be held on their future status. That was the point of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay, so that's your interpretation. Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, when you were making this first table on the ethnic composition of the population from the territory of the Republic of Serbia Krajina or, rather, UNPA, why didn't you use the Administrative Division of Croatia from that time? Why didn't you indicate them as municipalities that existed in 1991 or 1992, but used instead the latter administrative division which increased the number of existing municipalities by fragmenting them? As an expert, you should have used the administrative division from the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I could have used both. I chose to make this table to show the status of -- the current status of things concerning particular places, including Vukovar among others, because the current -- today's administrative division delimits the area of Vukovar town, whereas the previous administrative division was a much larger territory. You can see that precisely because of that, we had to divide the Vukovar-Srem county, and this was much more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, you gave us here data on the number of registered expelled persons, and displaced persons in Croatia. We have 27 March 1992 data and some other dates, later dates. But you provided us with information in table 6, "Overview of Facilities in Organised Accommodation and Number of Persons Accommodated in October 1992," and then a list of those facilities and the number of people put up in them. You have "B" category facilities, hotels; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you have a lower category, refugee centres, collective accommodation, and then another category where displaced persons are placed in private accommodation. When you look at the numbers, 73.898 in "B" category, then in a lower category you have the total 15.033, in refugee centres you have 21.020, and in facilities where only food is provided, that's 16.401 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I suppose you're looking for the table.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that this is at e-court -- the page number of the English is, I believe, 67, and the B/C/S is 50, just for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay is only seeking to interrupt me, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 73.000, and if we add to that 15.033, that's 103.921. Then we add 21.000, and that gives us -- let it be 130.000. Then we have 16.000 receiving only food. Let's say the total is 150.000, and I rounded it off to your benefit, in your favour. And then we have the registered number of displaced persons in Croatia as of the 27th March 1992, seven months earlier, that is, 325.806. I suppose in October, there must have been much more than 325.000. So if 150.000 were put up in hotels, collective centres, et cetera, what happened with the 200.000 who were not put up in that way? They were placed in Serbian houses and flats, if there were 325.000 in the first place? Where else would they have been put up? Perhaps somewhere with family, but not many could have been put up with family.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That is precisely where you are wrong. A large number of expelled persons, and later displaced persons, were not accommodated in an organised way. They were in private accommodation. To begin with, with family. Some people later moved to organised accommodation when we could provide more of it. But I mentioned that already in 1993, we started building large settlements for displaced persons, with the help of international donations and institutions, and 15 of such centres were built in Croatia, accommodating a large number of persons. So the accommodation facilities listed in this report were additionally increased. The largest number of people, whether we are talking about expelled persons or refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were the largest number, remained in private accommodation, first with friends and some found other ways later. As for the numbers, the numbers were very high in the beginning, because they had left their homes within the Republic of Croatia, and the largest number of those left their homes in 1991 and the beginning of 1992, when a large number of people left not only these occupied areas but also the areas of the Republic of Croatia that suffered from constant shelling. Part of those people were put up within Croatia, and others left the country. Just after the Sarajevo truce and the deployment of the UNPROFOR in UNPAs in the Republic of Croatia, a large number of these people returned to their homes. I also said that according to our legislation, we did not recognise these people as expelled. In the registration drive in April 1994, we defined very precisely --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are starting to talk about things that are not in the scope of my question. My time is precious, and I want to discuss many things with you. Croatian authorities, with regard to all Serbs who were expelled or who fled from the area of Croatia controlled by the Zagreb government, they annulled their housing rights, and even the international authorities had to intervene; correct? Are you going to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The Croatian authorities didn't do this, but the courts acted in this way in their judgements. There are court judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When I say "the Croatian government," well, I'm referring to the legislative, executive and local authorities, when I say "the Croatian authorities." Well, if these very bodies act differently, the Parliament, the executive body, the legislative body, well, I'm not interested in that. You represent the Croatian authorities, in my mind. You deprived the Serbs of their housing rights. I don't mean you, personally, when I say "you," but the Croatian authorities at various levels, and you allocated their flats to Croats. And the Serbs, who fled or were expelled, could no longer regain those housing rights; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in Croatia we have a programme. We have certain rules in force that we implement, and we are implementing them to this very day. According to these rules and regulations, people who lost their housing rights in Croatia, well, they can be allocated flats if they want to return to Croatia; and so in this way they can return to Croatia. This programme is being implemented. When it comes to large towns, well, in this manner we have provided about 750 families with accommodation. In the areas that are concerned by state social care, we've provided accommodation for about 5.000 families. They used to have housing rights. And in these areas of special interest or special care, the areas that were occupied, such as Knin, well, in those areas, in this manner, about 5.000 families have returned to those areas; to Vukovar, too. For example, out of 70 -- 70 per cent of them are Serbs. As far as these urban areas are concerned, the large towns like Zagreb and Osijek, well, I said that about 750 families had been provided with flats in this way, and this is something we're working on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, these are insignificant numbers in comparison with the hundreds of thousands expelled Serbs, but you should be aware that in the former Yugoslavia, having housing rights amounted to having certain property rights. A state would allocate a flat to you, or your company. An institution would allocate a flat to you, and then you could use that flat for life. No one could expel you. Your children could inherit it. You could exchange the flat. The only thing you couldn't do was sell it. So housing rights were different from property rights only in that you could not sell it; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, you're not right, and I think that many lawyers would not agree with what you have said. This is, in fact, a fairly significant legal subject that could be discussed at length; but I think that judgements could also be of assistance when it comes to this subject, judgements that were handed down a few years ago by the Court for Human Rights based in Strasbourg, in a very well-known case. Well, there was Blecic versus Croatia, this was a very well-known case, and there was a different interpretation of what you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm rather surprised, because earlier on you told us that you were not a lawyer, and now you're quoting decisions of the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. I'm rather taken aback by all this. But when it comes to social property now, I have the following question: If we take the case of a Serbian family that was expelled, that left Zagreb, and that had the use of a flat because they had been assigned this apartment by their company, what measures were taken by the Croatian government to restore the rights of these people, or is it the case that the Croatian government did nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous answer, I tried to explain this. It wasn't the subject of my report. These are things that we are working on at present. We would provide flats for people returning to the Republic of Croatia. We do this by allocating flats in areas of special interest to the state, and this is how we would make it possible for these people to return. Many of these people are in Serbia. They don't have any other property, and whether they are allocated a flat depends on whether they return to Croatia. In response to Mr. Seselj's question, I also provided some figures. About 5.000 families in the area of special state concern are concerned, and about 750 families outside the area of special state concern are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the flats that they had housing rights to are not returned to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need some clarification from the witness before you continue. You are referring to Tribunal decisions or rulings. Were they taken based on a new piece of legislation that changed the former act regarding usufruct; is that right, or did I not understand properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, as I have already pointed out, I'm not a lawyer; so I couldn't really make an assessment. But I am familiar with those judgements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this was not my question. I don't want you to go into legal details. I just wanted to know whether you knew whether there was a new act that would have changed the previous act removing the right of usufruct, and I wanted to know whether there was a law that was applied retractively. That's the only thing I want to know, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no retractive law was passed. But in 1996, the idea of housing rights came to an end; the system came to an end. Then certain deadlines were established, and deadlines by which one should try to sell the flat for which one had housing rights. So nothing was done retroactively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would seek another clarification, if you don't mind. You said that you had a programme aimed at helping Serbs who wanted to return to Croatia, so to help them to be resettled or find accommodation. I wanted to know whether that programme took on board their will or their choice as to the village or town where they wanted to return, or whether you had decided as to a special location where you would put all these people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We really took into account the desires that people had, where they wanted to return to. The first rule was that people would submit requests. Most people would submit a request to return to the place of residence they had in 1991, and this was something that we respect or this is something that we respect. Naturally, in some places it's easier to find accommodation. In other places, it's more difficult. But, in any event, we strive to respect people's desires, and on the whole people want to live in places where they lived in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the last payable, table 4, you provided information from the High Commission of the Office for Refugees. I believe that this is a reliable source. You provided information on the number of refugees registered in other republics of the former Yugoslavia. It's the 27th of March, 1992, in Serbia, 142.000; is that correct? Montenegro, Macedonia, several thousand; in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 95.000; and the total number is 252.000. This includes the 7.600 registered in Slavonia; 252.000 refugees from Croatia, and other republics of the former Yugoslavia; is that correct? On the whole, these people are Serbs; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. That's probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps there's a few Slovenians, a few Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: We cannot make such claims, since the information from that period -- well, we weren't the only ones to keep records. Other states did too. So no one kept precise records so that we could know exactly who is in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The UNHCR also registered these individuals on the basis of their ethnic origins, and the Serbian government did that. I can't say that Montenegro, Macedonia and Slovenia acted in a similar way, but the UNHCR did act in this way. There were naturally certain cases in which Croats came to Croatia from Serbia. I know a well-known Croatian intellectual, Goran Babic. Have you heard of him? He went to Serbia from Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, moved from Croatia to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- because he couldn't support Tudjman's regime, and when we examine those numbers, well the number of Croats would be very low. On the whole, we're dealing with some Serbs, perhaps some Muslims, but it's not clearly stated here. Perhaps there were Slovenians who fled during the war to Slovenia, and Macedonians who went to Macedonia, because 2.000 of them went to Macedonia. Out of 252.000, over 200.000 are Serbs. There's no doubt about that. That would be the minimum number. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's possible. Very well. And now we have the number of refugees from Croatia and other states, 115.781. You said that this information was gathered on the basis of the assessment of foreign countries, mostly on the basis of Germany's assessments. Do you have any information as to how many Serbs and how many Croats is included in this figure?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: What I know with regard to the information from that period of time, well, in two cases you have precise information. It concerns Switzerland and Czechoslovakia. But it was a problem at the time to determine whether someone was a Croat or a Serb; or, rather, to determine whether someone was a citizen of the Republic of Croatia or a citizen of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were all fleeing with the passport of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct. So for a long time, statistics were kept in many states according to which we were dealing with SFRY citizens. No distinctions were made as to whether someone was from Croatia or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's correct, but this is information for which you said that the refugees were from Croatia, so 115.781 individuals. Well, these individuals are from Croatia; that's what you've written down here?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: These are estimates of the authorities of the UNHCR, but that does not mean that there are no Serbs included in the figure. We can't make that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or the majority are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, because we're dealing with people who are from Croatia. Later on, when the process of returning from those foreign countries had started, we then saw that among those people, well, there were both Croats and Serbs. But we're talking about Croatian citizens. We can't keep records in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Croatian citizens, also that over 200.000 Serbs who fled from Croatia, over 150.000 went to Serbia and over 50.000 to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct? They are also Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct, they are Croatian citizens, Croatian nationals, because among them there are people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm looking at the time, because I want Mr. Seselj to be able to use his hour and a half. I don't want to interrupt him. I'm looking at the 164 individuals who went to Switzerland. Your department, your office, could have asked the UNHCR or the Swiss authorities to know how many of these 164 people would declare themselves as Serb or Croat. It wasn't that complicated to do, and you would have a fair estimation. Of course, you have 55.000 in Germany. It must be a mixture of Serbs and Croats, more complicated. But when you have smaller figures, it was easier to find out. There are 2.000 in Czechoslovakia, 2.117. It might have been interesting to look at the breakdown. Well, it wasn't done. It will remain at that. Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's see about the following: You have table 11. It's an overview of individuals who fled from Serbia from 1991 to 1995. For you, all these people who moved from Serbia to Croatia are refugees? All these people who moved from 1991 to 1995, they're refugees or expelled persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: We're dealing with people who were registered in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because Croatia provided certain financial benefits if one registered, so why shouldn't they register; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: As I have already explained, Croatia did not provide financial benefit, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For ease of reference, the e-court reference, I believe, is English page 114, B/C/S page 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have cited here, broken down by municipalities in Serbia, first of all you divided it into Serbia proper and Vojvodina and Kosovo; and then you stated precisely, municipality by municipality, what you registered, and I have no reason to doubt it in advance. And now we have numbers. From Serbia property, for a long time there is no movement towards Croatia almost at all; in 1991, 3; in 1992, 12; in 1993, 48; and then in 1996 it's 113. In total, we have 546 people who moved from Serbia to Croatia, and you keep them on record as refugees. There are 17 Serbs among them?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In total, it's 546 people. Now, let's look at Vojvodina. We have 5.131 persons there?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1990, 7; in 1991, 61. I draw the attention of the Chamber to this. It's very important. In all of 1990, 290 from Vojvodina; in 1993, 345; in 1994, 541; and in 1995, after Operations Flash and Storm, 1.868; in 1996, 280. In total, 5.131 persons moved from Vojvodina, all of Vojvodina, to Croatia. You registered them as refugees. Only 3.377 were Croats. That's your number; right?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: It's at least 3.377 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. There are at least 61 Serbs who moved from Vojvodina to Croatia. You register them -- you keep them on record as refugees. There are also six Muslims, in the category of "Others," 144; 32 unknown. But the total number is 5.131 persons from 1990 through 1996. And what happens in 1997? In 1997, you say the Croatian government established a state agency for the purchase of real estate. That state agency purchases Serbian property for peanuts and assigns it to Croats who move from anywhere to Croatia; is that correct? You can answer with a "yes" or "no" so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this, because it is not a simple matter, and it is not assigned only and exclusively to Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't like complicated matters, so let's move on. We have this information from Vojvodina, but what will be of special interest to the Judges, I suppose, because you showed considerable diligence and conscientiousness in the substance of this report, you should remember 5.131 people moved from Vojvodina to Croatia, including 61 Serbs. And now look what happens? From Kosovo and Metohija, the total is 6.924 persons who moved to Croatia. Out of them, 3.755 Croats, 7 Serbs, 91 Muslims, and others, 1.490. That must include the Gornji, Turks, Albanians, et cetera. From whom or what did they flee from Kosovo? The largest number, look at how they left. Before 1996, it says "4.251," which means we don't know exactly when they left, and then year by year, the figures are much smaller: 1990, 14; 1992, 27; 1993, 670. They left certainly before 1996, but we don't know when, 4.251. In total, it's 6.924. So it's 1.800 more than from Vojvodina. From what did they flee from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: As you could see from these numbers for yourself, concerning these people from Kosovo, they are mainly Croats, but not exclusively Croats. There were a lot of Albanians among them who left before 1995, but also after 1995, and moved to Croatia. The largest number came to Croatia in 1999, during the war in Kosovo, and among them there was a large number of Albanians and -- Croats and Albanians. And people were also leaving for the reasons we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fleeing in the face of certain dangers?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: Among these 5.131 people -- or let's reduce it. Among 3.755 Croats, who according to your data fled from Vojvodina to Croatia, how many left without having exchanged their property; that is, abandoning their flats and houses in Serbia without exchanging them? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information here. Some of the figures reflecting in what housing they are is recorded with our agency, but I did not include it in the report because I didn't search for numbers according to that criterion. But we recorded the situation when they registered. So I cannot tell you the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, you have a total of 3.377 Croats that you say fled from Serbia between 1991 and 1999, with a proviso that before 1992 -- that is, until 1992, in 1991 and 1992 together, the number was 358? Did I do the addition right?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 358 Croats who fled from Vojvodina to Croatia. What should be the most important for us here, in your expert report, would have been if you had found whether, among them, there was a single Croat who had to flee from Serbia for any reason, leaving all their real estate behind, all their immovable property. I say that it's not the case. All of them either sold their property and left or exchanged their property and left. Nobody had to run away in haste. I know that in some war-stricken areas, people had literally to flee, to run away, carrying only a little bag, but in Serbia it never happened. Nobody had to run with just a small bag. Now, can I please know how much time is left to me, because I'll have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You need to make it brief, because we need to have at least ten minutes before the end of the hearing for housekeeping matters. Let me see. You have used one hour, so you must have 30 minutes left. Witness, just one question, because these figures are extremely relevant for us. They are indeed at the very centre of the indictment regarding Vojvodina. I'm focusing on 1991 and 1992. With regard to, well, first 1990, we have seven leaving. Well, not much happened in 1990. We have 61 for 1991 and 290 for 1992. As part of your survey, it would have been interesting to know how many people had actually exchanged their flats or apartments out of these 350, because if 350 exchanged apartments in complete freedom, that's different as in a situation where you're forced to do so. In 1993, we have 345, and then we can see that the situation is deteriorating because the next year is 541, and then 1.800 the following year. But we're focusing on 1991 and 1992, and it would have been interesting to know, out of the 350, how many exchanged apartments. But I don't suppose you have an answer. You don't have any doubt on that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, I have no numbers showing how many people had exchanged their property. The numbers that we have, but I did not derive them for this report in particular, are the numbers showing reasons for leaving that people stated during registration. In most cases, they mentioned expulsion and personal threats or harassment as the reasons for leaving their homes. There is another important proviso; namely, that a significant number of these people did not register as refugees. Here I'm only talking about people who registered as refugees and obviously had reasons to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have five minutes before the break, so you have time before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to draw your attention, Mr. President, concerning these 350 from Vojvodina up to the end of 1992. Information on their ethnic composition would have been interesting, because not all of them were Croats. There could have been Serbs among those 350, if there were 61 Serbs from this area motivated by something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that 127.000 Serbs, according to your files that you opened returned to the area of -- to the territory of Croatia. A few days ago, Serbian authorities informed the public that around 75.000 returned. How do you interpret this? How do you explain this difference of 52.000 in Serb returnees?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I can only talk about the people who registered as returnees to the Republic of Croatia, and this is an exact number, 127.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You gave us information about the age composition, gender percentages, very detailed information broken down by municipalities in Croatia, about Croats who fled from somewhere to Croatia; but it would have been interesting to know the age composition of the Serbs that you have on your files as having returned. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Our agency does have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did not deem it necessary to include it in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't asked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because the Prosecution is not interested in the fate of Serbs. You're right, they always represent your side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw my objection. That is my comment. Let's move on, so Ms. Biersay shouldn't jump so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, it is mostly Serbs who are elderly, who are simply unable to start a new life anywhere or get used to a new place, or who came back to finally sell their property at any price and then leave the area now under Croatian control, am I right that these are mostly elderly people or people who are coming only in order to sell their property?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: You cannot talk about it in such an exclusive way. A large number, higher than in other segments of population, are elderly people. Why? Because elderly people are the first to come back. But that's no longer the case. You have many more younger families with children coming back to Croatia. This story that it's mainly elderly people coming back or people who want to sell their property, that happened in the beginning, because in all situations that results in refugees, among all ethnic groups, Serbs, Croats, any others, elderly people are the first to come back. Younger people come back later. So you can't be that exclusive. Of course, in this number there is a larger number of Serbs, and some of them, of course, came to sell their property. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, explain this miracle. In 1997, the Croatian government established a state agency for the purchase of real estate. I know of no other example in Europe where a state, a country, establishes an agency to purchase the real estate of its own nationals who want to get rid of it. That's what happened in Croatia in 1997. I would understand if it was left to some special funds, or foundations, or local self-government, but you have a special state agency dealing with purchase of Serbian property for peanuts; and I know this for a fact, it's for peanuts. I have reliable information about this. Can you explain that, as an expert?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: This agency, I didn't know you were going to ask this, so I didn't take the papers with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you expect me to ask?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I can tell you a few things about that agency. It was established at the time of the peaceful reintegration of Croatian Podunavlje when, among other things, an agreement was made on two-way return from Croatian Podunavlje to other areas of Croatia, and vice versa. This agreement deals with the return of internally-displaced persons. In that agreement, the possibility of selling property is mentioned, and this agency is also mentioned. This agreement - I'm sorry, I don't have it with me - was signed between the Croatian government and the transitional administration. It provides the possibility of people who remained in Croatian Podunavlje, of deciding whether they want to stay, and if they want to go, whether they want to sell their property. And that agency served the purpose of buying their property, because in that area at the time there was no real estate market.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But a large number of Serbs is not returning. You say that certain areas of Croatia. You mean actually the Republic of Serbian Krajina or UNPAs were liberated by Operation Storm in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was liberated from all the Serbian population, because all Serbs were expelled. Those who were not expelled were killed. Those who were foolish enough to stay were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't. Very well, you can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break for 20 minutes and resume at 20 past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Registrar has told me that Mr. Seselj has 22 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, do you know that the majority of the refugees and expelled Serbs, especially those who were expelled at the time of Flash and Storm, simply don't want to return to their homes for as long as the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in which they lived, is not liberated? Are you aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I know that there are many Serbs who fled from Croatia and have decided not to return to the Republic of Croatia, but I cannot speculate as to the reasons for this. International investigations carried out by the OSS, the UNHCR and other organisation show that there are various reasons for which some decided to return and some decided not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. In the concluding parts of your report, you do not attempt to use a scientific or specialist method in order to analyse certain themes. You have recourse to journalist method, and you described your view of the alleged expulsion of Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. As an example, I'll mention the case of Borovo Selo. You say that Croatian policemen were killed and massacred there. One might draw the conclusion that Serbian terrorists killed innocent Croatian policemen; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Here I'm only referring to an event that took place in that area, an event the consequence of which was the departure of a certain number of non-Serbs from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, I read through that carefully. You said that they were killed and massacres; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I'll tell you what I know about the event, since volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party participated in the fighting there, and today they are proud of that victory, and so am I, who sent them there. I'm proud of that Serbian victory. The Serbian villages in eastern part of Slavonia and in Srem were under threat because various Croatian military formation were attacking them. The Serbs were unlawfully arrested and beaten up, and some of them were even killed. And as a result, the Serbian villages set up blockades at access routes, and they used weapons to prevent the Croatian police and paramilitary formations from entering these places. Then there were negotiations to calm the situation down. Reihl Kir participated in the negotiations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please refrain from testifying and put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't put my question to the witness until I inform the witness of what happened there, according to the information I had. But, Ms. Lattanzi, you should have noticed that many parts of this expert report amount to no more than a journalistic view of the events. The Croats are always innocent and the Serbs are guilty. And this wasn't the task assigned to the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another matter, Mr. Seselj. Your questions should refer to the various parts of your description, because you start by referring to all sorts of events, you describe a whole series of events, and then at the end we have no idea what your question is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not interested in the event, so I won't deal with it. History has recorded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am interested, indeed. You cannot say that I'm not interested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... thanks. How did the Croatian policemen enter this Serbian village? There were peace negotiations, an agreement was reached to calm things down and to remove the blockades. The blockades were removed, and then the Croatian policemen entered Borovo Selo, armed to the teeth, and they were bussed in. As soon as they got out of the buses, they opened fire. The Serbs responded and they won. And now one says in this expert report that innocent Croatian policemen were killed. And this is an expert for refugees and displaced persons. That was the substance of my question, but I will abandon that question. I don't have anymore time to deal with, so I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Borovo Selo is a very significant event, indeed. You mention that in your report. Mr. Seselj has just given us his version of the events that took place there. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This event, and other similar events in Croatia, well, regardless of the causes - I can't go into the causes, I'm not such an expert - but I only mention these events here as events that actually took place, and I describe them such as they were described. I say that these people were killed not only in the course of combat. I say that there was a massacre too. There are several such events that took place in various parts of Croatia, and as a result of these events, a certain number of the population fled from the area concerned. In the case of Borovo Selo, the outskirts of the town of Vukovar, the settlement of Borovo and Vukovar, strictly speaking, well, in those cases the first refugees started appearing in certain areas of Croatia. They came from areas where such events took place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, while combat was still ongoing, a tank unit from the JNA intervened and put an end to the armed conflict. They helped the Croats to get out, to withdraw, and to withdraw with their dead and with the wounded. That's for your information, but it's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why doesn't your report, Ms. Radic, cover the Serbs who, after Storm and Flash, moved to Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, although there were quite a few of them?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Because I wasn't requested to cover that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. That satisfies me as an answer. Do you know that between two censuses in Croatia in 1991 and 2001, a discrepancy of -- a minority -- a loss of 38.000 Serbs was recorded? So even if we don't take into account -- we shouldn't take into account the idea that the birth rate was nil for the Serbs. Children must have been born. That was the case for the Croats, that was the case for the Serbs. There's no difference in the birth rate; there shouldn't be any difference.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So 38.000 [as interpreted] Serbs were missing between these two censuses; you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. There's a mistake in the transcript. It's 380.000, and not 38.000. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everyone's against me here, even the court reporter, but it doesn't matter. I'm used to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are here to control everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you answer this question, Ms. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the censuses, and that is correct, 380.000 -- 380.000 and 32 between the two censuses. But the census was in 2001, and after 2001 we, as a body, dealt with the return of refugees, registered 40.000 returnees. They had returned from abroad. So the figure is a little different in relation to the one mentioned in the census. That's one thing, but this is just a census. Just allow me to say one more thing. It would be important to compare the areas that were directly affected by the war, areas where the entire non-Serbian population, on the one side, started fleeing, and afterwards the Serbian population started fleeing from such areas; so this is the sphere that this body that I lead deals with. As a result of the war and all the events, both segments of the population emigrated. We don't have fewer Serbs; we also have fewer Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. First the Serbs started fleeing as early as 1990, after Tudjman's regime was established. There was the return of Ustasha symbols. There were homeland certificates that were introduced. That's when the Serbs started fleeing, first urban Serbs -- well, you should have consulted Svetozar Livada, who has information about that.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecution also has such information. Very well. In this information that you have on Croatian refugees, well, there were lots of Croats who fled from Bosnia and Herzegovina included in this information; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: In the information I present in my report, apart from several places where refugees are explicitly referred to, well, in this information we're dealing with citizens of the Republic of Croatia. We're not talking about Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. In several places, Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina are mentioned. Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina are not included in the figure of 220.000 expelled persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When Tudjman's regime was established, all the Croats obtained the right to have Croatian nationality, and many Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina used their right; and they participated in all Croatian elections on a massive scale in the previous 18 years; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So almost all of them. I don't know who didn't, but almost all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the same time citizens of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot agree with you. That's not the case for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But almost all of them are. Whoever didn't want to be a citizen of Croatia didn't become such a citizen. There were those who adhered to the Muslim regime in Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's my claim, but it doesn't matter. Would it be correct to say that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, before the war, the Croats represented 17 per cent of the population, according to the official statistics?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that as things stand today, they represent less than 6 per cent, not even 6 per cent of the population; you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I can't provide you with any precise figures. Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't carry out a census. We're just talking about estimates here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. You know that the Croatian government filed charges against Serbia for allegedly committing acts of genocide, they filed these charges with ICJ?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In order to put my following question to you, I'll tell you a little historical anecdote. Towards the end of 1941 or at the beginning of 1942, the American President Roosevelt called the most prominent politicians from Serbian Croatia to Washington. Jovan Ducic, one of the greatest Serbian poets, attended. Juri Krnjevic was the most distinguished Croat, the vice-president of the Croatian Peasant Party, and Macek's first deputy. There was much discussion on the Ustasha crimes, crimes committed by the Ustasha against the Serbian people, and terrible news about such crimes had already arrived in America. The Croats who attended tried to deny those crimes and to ascribe those crimes to Italian or German occupiers. I'll conclude in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution would object to Mr. Seselj essentially testifying. If he has a question for the witness, he should just pose it. The pretence that he's going through, giving a speech and then asking a question at the end, is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but before you put a question, you have to lay the foundation. Mr. Seselj wants to put a question to the witness about a meeting between Mr. Roosevelt, a Serb and a Croat. That's what he's explaining. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also have to put slightly complex questions to experts, not simple questions as is the case for witnesses who have only completed primary school. Ms. Radic is an expert here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Given the attempts to conceal the Ustasha crimes and ascribe guilt to Germans and Italians -- or when doing this, Jovan Ducic said the following. He said: "You Croats are the most courageous people in the world, but not because you're not afraid of anyone. You Croats are the most courageous people in the world because you're not ashamed of anything." Ms. Radic, given the way the Croatian government acted, and given the charges against Serbia, have Ducic's words just been emphasised, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The microphone was switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have now concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you repeat your answer. We had a slight technical hitch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, I don't see any relation between those words and that event or, rather, the proceedings that are ongoing. I think that this is more a matter of someone's opinion, not a matter of fact. I can only speak about facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question, following something Mr. Seselj asked you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are an educated witness, so I can put a long or longer or more complex question to you than to a less-educated person. We had a number of witnesses who told us that a lot of Serbs arrived in Vojvodina from Croatia. We were given a great deal of detailed evidence about all this. We heard that apartments were exchanged, but I'm not going to go into more detail about this. Earlier on, Mr. Seselj talked about the census of 1991 and the census of 2001. And according to him, and I suppose he's relying on very reliable documents, we find a deficit of over 300.000 Serbs between the two censuses, between the census of 1991 and between the census of 2001. This is a very high figure indeed, 300.000 people who, in 2001, did not register as Serbs. This is your area of expertise. Could you tell us if these figures are accurate? Do they reflect the truth or the reality?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: These numbers that reflect the shortfall in population between two censuses are correct. There has been a lot of debate about why. There was a decrease not only in the number of Serbs in Croatia, if we are speaking now about the ethnic composition of the population, there was also a decrease in the number of Croats. Between these two censuses, the methodology of census has also changed considerably, and there has been a lot of debate and public opinion about that. The numbers are correct, but if we were to talk about the reasons, then we would need special analysis, because we're talking demographics here. You must know that at this time the birth rate should also be taken into account, and in that period, the birth rate was negative for all the ethnic communities. And between the two censuses, not only because of the war, we had a large migration of the population not only from Croatia, not only of Serbs and Croats, towards third countries. There was the phenomenon of "brain drain"; that is, the move of young, educated people to the West. Some people also left as refugees. Many people are still living in the Netherlands, for example, and are not even planning to go back. It's not only Serbs; it's a lot of Croats as well. That's how the population decreased. Also, indubitably, the war had a large impact on the demographics in Croatia, and not only in Croatia but specifically on the areas that were stricken by the war and occupied, because from there almost the entire non-Serb population fled, and after them the Serbs fled too. Our demographers wrote a lot about it, and there are numerous papers dealing with these events. These papers attempt to explain the reasons why it all happened and in what period the Serbs left these areas. It is difficult for me to speak about that, because there's four, or in the case of a certain area, seven years, we have no way of knowing how many people left the Republic of Croatia at the time because we had no control over the border, and we don't know why these people were leaving. All we know is that they did leave. The fact, however, is that today, despite all the measures our government is taking, enabling people to find new housing in those areas, and to return, and to enable the return of the prewar population to those areas, both Serbs and Croats, we still have a shortfall of 65 per cent compared to the census. But since it's been seven years from the census, if we add to this figure the number of returnees, we still have a shortfall of at least 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question. What is the population today in Croatia, how many inhabitants, and how many Serbs in that population?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: According to the census, four and a half million I believe is the total population. According to that census, there were 4.5 per cent. But as I said, the return of refugees continued even after the census.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to the 1991 census, there were 12 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. That was the question that I was about to ask. You were ahead of me. I was about to ask the following: In 1991, how many inhabitants were there, and what was the percentage of Serbs in that population?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: 4.700.000, and the percentage of Serbs was 12.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a drop in the percentage with regard to the Serbs. There's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to cover, very briefly, two areas, and the first area that I'd like to discuss with you is the statistics and numbers with respect to refugees from Vojvodina. And the second area - there will be some overlap - has to do with the definitions that we have been discussing, and hopefully we can clarify some issues and not muddle it further. With respect to those individuals coming from Vojvodina, as refugees, into Croatia, now, this table 11 to your report gives us some figures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's organised by dates. Do those years at the top of the table represent the date of expulsion or something else?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: They represent the date of expulsion, and concerning a number of persons for whom we had no information of this date, we have the date of registration; namely, dates of expulsion were taken from the personal statements of people who stated that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that is what I'd like to ask you. Where does that information come from, the expulsion date?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: It comes from the registration of expelled persons in 1994, and we keep these records electronically from that time onwards. During that registration drive, everyone signed a certain form, signed it, and made a statement indicating when they were expelled and the reasons of expulsion. Of course, all the other information concerning their accommodation was also included, and they received IDs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. In all the documentation here in the table, we see references to refugees, whereas Ms. Biersay speaks of expelled persons, and the witness picks it up and speaks of dates of expulsion. I have just seen this table. I can find it again. The reference there is to refugees from the area of Serbia, and a distinguishment is made between Serbia property, Vojvodina and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the record. The Judges keep all of this in mind, whatever the questions. There's no way you can misdirect us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if an individual, say, from Vojvodina sought refuge in Croatia, let's say, in 1992, and that person did register with one of the local centres, if that person then left before the re-registration in 1994, would that person appear in the data that's contained in table 11?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: That person would not appear there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Because the paper trail of approving somebody's status was exclusively on the local level until 1994. It was kept in centres for social security, that was a local organisation, and in regional offices. They kept the archives, but only in hard copy. So the information on persons who had the status in 1992 and 1993 were never collected in one place that would give us a list of names. That is why in 1994, we organised this re-registration so that we could have, in one place, a list and all the information on all the persons who were then recorded as displaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then my final question pertains to the geographical coverage, if you will, of some of these terms that we've been using; namely, "refugees." Are refugees people who are displaced within the Republic of Croatia or people who are coming from outside of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA-MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Refugees are people who arrived from other states, other countries; that is, either from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Serbia. They are not the same as internally displaced within the borders of Croatia. If we are talking about people who fled within the borders of the Republic of Croatia, we speak of expelled persons. The international term frequently used is a synonym, but that could only cause confusion in the courtroom, is "internally displaced." And in order to understand this better, the term in English is used "displaced."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, please. These are internally-displaced persons, as we say in Serbia, and tendentiously the Croats introduced the term "expelled persons," whereas "expelled" means people who were deported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've devoted a lot of time to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I've completed the redirect, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Witness, for testifying on behalf of the Prosecution. I wish you a safe return home, and I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. I have a few administrative matters. Some will be in open session, others in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, Mr. Seselj, this is a question for you.
